subject: Career
title: The Art of the Warm Introduction
description: A quick, practical guide to The Art of the Warm Introduction.

hook.text: A mutual friend says: 'You two should meet.' That warm intro is 10x more powerful than a cold email.

buildup.text: Warm introductions carry borrowed trust. The connector's reputation is on the line.

discovery.text: The double opt-in intro is the gold standard: ask both parties before connecting them.

twist.text: Requesting intros without context puts your connector in an awkward position. Give them the 'why.'

climax.text: Make it easy: 'Could you intro me to Sara? I want to ask about her team's approach to X.'

punchline.text: Cold opens doors. Warm introductions open them wider.

quiz.question: What is the double opt-in introduction?
options: Asking both parties before connecting them

details.summary: A warm introduction, where a mutual contact vouches for you, carries exponentially more trust than a cold approach. The quality of the introduction depends on the introducer's credibility and the specificity of the endorsement.
details.whyItMatters: Warm introductions bypass the trust deficit that kills most cold outreach. They transfer the introducer's social capital to you, dramatically accelerating relationship formation.
takeaways: Always make it easy for your introducer to forward your request
Provide a concise blurb about yourself the introducer can paste
Thank both the introducer and the recipient promptly afterward

faq.question: How do you ask someone for a warm introduction without being pushy?
faq.answer: Frame it as optional and make their effort minimal. Say 'Would you be comfortable introducing me to X? I have written a brief blurb you can forward if it makes it easier. No pressure at all if the timing is not right.' This respects their relationship capital.

faq.question: What should the blurb you provide to your introducer include?
faq.answer: Include who you are in one sentence, a specific and legitimate reason for the meeting, and a clear low-commitment ask. Keep it under sixty words so the introducer can paste it directly without editing.
